catalog_quote: Like the vast majority of Niger-Congo languages, Mambay is tonal. All syllables in all utterances are affected by tone, and its behaviour in the language is systematic. ... Two contrastive tone levels are found in Mambay: H (high) and L (low). Tones from these two levels are organized into contrastive tone melodies and associated with morphemes or, in some cases, phonological words (4.1). ... Four major processes affect the tone system. While tone deletion is a lexical process, postlexical processes consist of downstep, H tone spread and L tone spread (4.3). ... [§4.2.3, p. 131:] There is no significant interaction between tone and phonological structures other than the TBUs with which they are associated. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Mambay is described as a two-level (H/L) tone language with lexical tone melodies, downstep, tone spread and intonational register shift; the full phonology (516 pp.) and the JIPA Illustration posit no word stress or accent and make no statement about stress at all.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress analysis); register shift for emphasis operates on morphemes, not syllables (JIPA p.231)
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word defined as domain of one tonal melody (§2.5 p.95); tone processes bounded by phonological phrase. No stress domain given because no stress is described.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Mambay [mcs] as spoken around Figuil/Bibemi (North Province, Cameroon) and Mayo-Kebbi (Chad); Anonby notes little dialect variation. Same language as Glottolog mamb1294 'Mambai'.

sources.note: Nothing. Chapters 2-4 (segments, syllable/word structure, nasality, tone and intonation) contain no section or statement on stress/accent; 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the prosodic sense anywhere in the 516-page text. Ch. 4 (p.118) states Mambay is tonal with two levels H and L, seven lexical melodies, downstep, H/L tone spread, and intonational register shift; 4.2.3 (p.131) says there is no significant interaction between tone and other phonological structures. Word = domain of a single tonal melody (2.5, p.95).
